title: Act Decisively
author: John McLean
summary: John McLean's Wisdom From Dad issue 27 takes the tenet "Act Decisively" and ties it to a dad's job of raising decision-makers. He opens with Norway's World Cup run and its fans' imaginary Viking rowing as examples of someone simply acting on an idea. He recalls his own mentor Bob Proctor teaching him that a goal without action is just a wish. The centrepiece is Eisenhower's choice on June 5, 1944 to launch D-Day despite uncertain weather, and the note accepting blame he wrote in case it failed. McLean's lesson is that you can control the decision but not the outcome, so certainty is the wrong goal. For fathers, he argues that making every decision for your kids prevents them from learning, and he offers a four-question practice for working through a pending decision together.
points: Planning has to stop at some point; gathering more information can become a way of postponing the risk of deciding.
Eisenhower studied the situation, listened to his commanders, then decided and wrote a note taking responsibility if the invasion failed.
The goal is not certainty but the best decision available, followed by willingness to move forward and adjust.
Dads cannot raise competent decision makers by making every decision for their children.
The four questions (what do I know, what are my options, what is the best decision now, what is my first action) work for a father and his kids alike.
quotes: One of the easiest traps to fall into is continuing to gather information because making the decision feels riskier than preparing for it. Sometimes we tell ourselves we’re being thorough when, in reality, we’re simply postponing the moment when we have to act.
The goal isn’t certainty. The goal is to gather the best information available, make the best decision you can with what you know, and then be willing to move forward.

Acting decisively doesn’t mean waiting until you’re certain. It means gathering the best information you can, recognizing what you can and cannot control, and then making the decision and moving forward.
He understood that he could control the decision, but he couldn’t control the outcome. He was prepared to accept responsibility for the decision and move forward.
We can’t develop competent decision makers by making every decision for our kids. It’s tempting to do it; I know, because I did a lot of that while my kids were growing up.
It’s not by knowing you’ll always make the right decision, but by knowing you can make a decision, deal with the consequences and adjust when necessary.
A lighthouse doesn’t tell a sailor exactly where to go. It provides a fixed point in uncertain waters.
